questions.learningObjective: Identify the SI base unit for time
questions.stem: In the chef's recipe costing sheet, a timer logs elapsed cooking seconds; which SI base unit measures that time?

options.text: The second is the SI base unit for time in every standard recipe timer.
The minute is the SI base unit for time in every standard recipe timer.
options.misconception: treats derived minute as base unit

options.text: The hour is the SI base unit for time in every standard recipe timer.
options.misconception: treats derived hour as base unit

options.text: Time is measured in newtons in this costing sheet, not seconds.
options.misconception: confuses force unit with time unit

questions.explanation: The SI base unit for time is the second. Minutes and hours are derived units, and newtons measure force, so only the first option is correct.
questions.hint: Time base unit is the second.

questions.learningObjective: Convert kilograms to grams using prefix scale
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet lists a 2.5 kilogram bag of flour; how many grams is that?

options.text: 25 grams, found by moving the decimal one place right.
2500 grams, because kilo means one thousand.
250 grams, treating kilo as one hundred.
25000 grams, treating kilo as ten thousand.

questions.explanation: Kilo denotes a factor of one thousand, so 2.5 kg equals 2500 g. The other options misapply the prefix power.

questions.learningObjective: Convert metres per second to kilometres per hour
questions.stem: A costing sheet converts 10 metres per second to 3.6 kilometres per hour; what error was made?

options.text: No error; 10 m/s truly equals 3.6 km/h.
The factor was inverted; 10 m/s equals 36 km/h.
The units cancel incorrectly, giving 100 km/h.
Seconds were treated as hours, giving 600 km/h.

questions.explanation: Multiplying by 3.6 converts m/s to km/h, so 10 m/s is 36 km/h. The sheet used the reciprocal and is wrong.

questions.topic: Average speed from a trip log
questions.learningObjective: Compute average speed from distance and time
questions.stem: A recipe delivery trip covers 120 kilometres in 2 hours; what is the average speed in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is total distance divided by total time, so 120 km / 2 h = 60 km/h.

questions.stem: In a chef's costing sheet, acceleration is claimed to have dimensions of length over time squared; is that right?

options.text: Yes, acceleration has dimensions L T^-2.
No, acceleration has dimensions L T^-1, like speed.
No, acceleration has dimensions L^2 T^-2.
No, acceleration has dimensions M L T^-2, like force.

questions.explanation: Acceleration is change in velocity per time, giving L T^-2. Speed is L T^-1 and force is M L T^-2.
questions.hint: Acceleration is velocity change per time.

questions.stem: A velocity in the costing sheet is recorded with units m/s; what are its dimensions?

options.text: L T^-2, the dimensions of acceleration.
L T^-1, length divided by time.
L^2 T^-1, length squared over time.
M L T^-1, mass times velocity.

questions.explanation: Velocity is length over time, so its dimensions are L T^-1. The other choices add or change dimensions.

questions.topic: Dimensional test of a surface formula
questions.learningObjective: Test dimensional consistency of a surface formula
questions.stem: A costing sheet claims area equals length times time; which dimensional flaw does that show?

options.text: Area needs length squared, not length times time.
Area needs length cubed, not length times time.
Area needs mass times length, not length times time.
No flaw; length times time is area.

questions.explanation: Area has dimensions L^2, while length times time has L T, so the formula is dimensionally wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret newtons per kilogram as acceleration
questions.stem: A costing sheet lists a force of 40 newtons on a 5 kilogram mass; what is the resulting acceleration in m/s^2?
questions.explanation: Acceleration equals force divided by mass, so 40 N / 5 kg = 8 m/s^2.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish base unit from derived unit for time
questions.stem: Chef's costing sheet records a bake time of 45 minutes; is minute an SI base unit?

options.text: Yes, minute is one of the seven SI base units.
No, minute is derived; the base unit is the second.
No, minute is derived; the base unit is the hour.
Yes, but only for cooking measurements.

questions.explanation: Minute is not an SI base unit; time's base unit is the second. Hours are also derived.
questions.hint: Base unit for time is second.

questions.stem: The costing sheet shows 750 milligrams of spice; how many grams is that?

options.text: 75 grams, treating milli as centi.
0.75 grams, because milli means one thousandth.
7.5 grams, treating milli as one hundredth.
7500 grams, treating milli as ten.

questions.explanation: Milli means one thousandth, so 750 mg = 0.75 g. The other options misapply the prefix.
questions.hint: Milli means divide by one thousand.

questions.stem: A costing sheet converts 72 km/h to 20 m/s; is this conversion correct?

options.text: Yes, 72 km/h equals 20 m/s exactly.
No, 72 km/h equals 2 m/s.
No, 72 km/h equals 200 m/s.
No, 72 km/h equals 20 m/s but units are wrong.

questions.explanation: Dividing 72 by 3.6 gives 20 m/s, so the conversion is correct. The other options misplace decimals.

questions.topic: Average speed from a trip log
questions.learningObjective: Compute average speed with mixed units
questions.stem: A delivery covers 90 km in 1.5 hours; what is the average speed in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is 90 km / 1.5 h = 60 km/h.

questions.learningObjective: Identify correct acceleration formula by dimensions
questions.stem: In the costing sheet, two formulas for acceleration are offered; which is dimensionally valid?

options.text: a = v / t has dimensions L T^-2 and is valid.
a = v * t has dimensions L and is valid.
a = t / v has dimensions T^2 L^-1 and is valid.
a = v + t is valid because both are motion quantities.

questions.explanation: Acceleration is velocity change over time, so a = v/t gives L T^-2. Adding or multiplying mismatched dimensions is invalid.

questions.stem: A costing sheet uses v^2 in a formula; what are the dimensions of velocity squared?

options.text: L^2 T^-2, length squared over time squared.
L T^-2, length over time squared.
L^2 T^-1, length squared over time.
2 L T^-1, doubles the dimension.

questions.explanation: Squaring velocity squares both dimensions, giving L^2 T^-2. Exponents are not multipliers.

questions.topic: Dimensional test of a surface formula
questions.learningObjective: Reject a dimensionally inconsistent area formula
questions.stem: A costing sheet proposes area = mass times length; what is wrong with it?

options.text: Area should be length squared, not mass times length.
Area should be mass squared, not mass times length.
Area should be length times time, not mass times length.
Nothing; mass times length can be area.

questions.explanation: Area has dimensions L^2, so mass times length is dimensionally invalid. Mass is irrelevant to area.

questions.learningObjective: Compute weight from mass and g
questions.stem: A 3 kilogram ingredient has weight in newtons on Earth; what is it using g = 9.8 m/s^2?
questions.explanation: Weight equals mass times g, so 3 kg * 9.8 m/s^2 = 29.4 N.

questions.stem: Chef's costing sheet converts 1 hour to 3600 seconds; what makes this valid?

options.text: It uses 60 minutes per hour and 60 seconds per minute.
It uses 100 minutes per hour and 36 seconds per minute.
It uses 24 minutes per hour and 150 seconds per minute.
It is invalid because hours are base units.

questions.explanation: One hour is 60 minutes and each minute is 60 seconds, giving 3600 seconds. The other factors are wrong.

questions.stem: The costing sheet shows 250 centimetres of pastry; how many metres is that?

options.text: 25 metres, treating centi as deci.
2.5 metres, because centi means one hundredth.
0.25 metres, treating centi as one thousandth.
2500 metres, treating centi as ten.

questions.explanation: Centi means one hundredth, so 250 cm = 2.5 m. The other options misapply the prefix.

questions.learningObjective: Convert m/s to km/h with decimals
questions.stem: A costing sheet converts 5.5 m/s to 19.8 km/h; is that correct?

options.text: Yes, 5.5 times 3.6 is 19.8.
No, it should be 1.53 km/h.
No, it should be 55 km/h.
No, it should be 198 km/h.

questions.explanation: Multiplying 5.5 m/s by 3.6 gives 19.8 km/h, so the conversion is correct.

questions.topic: Average speed from a trip log
questions.learningObjective: Compute average speed from total distance and time
questions.stem: A trip log shows 200 km covered in 4 hours; what is the average speed in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is 200 km / 4 h = 50 km/h.

questions.stem: A costing sheet gives acceleration in metres per second; what unit is missing?

options.text: No unit is missing; m/s is correct for acceleration.
Seconds squared in denominator; m/s^2 is correct.
Metres squared in numerator; m^2/s is correct.
Kilograms in numerator; kg m/s is correct.

questions.explanation: Acceleration is m/s^2, so m/s is missing a second in the denominator. The other units are wrong.

questions.stem: In the costing sheet, a ratio of two speeds is computed; what are its dimensions?

options.text: L T^-1, same as a single speed.
Dimensionless, because units cancel.
L^2 T^-2, because two velocities multiply.
T L^-1, inverse of speed.

questions.explanation: Dividing two velocities cancels length and time, giving a dimensionless ratio. The other choices mishandle cancellation.

questions.topic: Dimensional test of a surface formula
questions.stem: A costing sheet claims surface area = 2 * length * width + 2 * length * height; dimensions?

options.text: L^2, since each term is length squared.
L^3, since area includes height.
L, since terms add linearly.
Dimensionless, since coefficients cancel units.

questions.explanation: Each term is length times length, L^2, so the sum is L^2. Coefficients are dimensionless.

questions.stem: A costing sheet lists 12 N/kg; how many m/s^2 is that?
questions.explanation: One newton per kilogram equals one metre per second squared, so 12 N/kg = 12 m/s^2.

questions.stem: Which quantity among time, length, mass, current, temperature, amount, luminosity is not an SI base?

options.text: All seven listed are SI base quantities.
Time is not an SI base quantity.
Mass is not an SI base quantity.
Length is not an SI base quantity.

questions.explanation: All seven listed are SI base quantities, including time. None is excluded.

questions.stem: A costing sheet lists 2 gigagrams of flour; how many grams is that?

options.text: 2,000 grams, treating giga as kilo.
2,000,000 grams, treating giga as mega.
2,000,000,000 grams, because giga means 10^9.
20 grams, treating giga as deca.

questions.explanation: Giga denotes 10^9, so 2 Gg = 2,000,000,000 g. The other options misapply the prefix.

questions.learningObjective: Convert m/s to km/h for a recipe robot
questions.stem: A costing sheet converts 8 m/s to 28.8 km/h for a delivery robot; correct?

options.text: Yes, 8 times 3.6 is 28.8.
No, it should be 2.22 km/h.
No, it should be 80 km/h.
No, it should be 288 km/h.

questions.explanation: Multiplying 8 m/s by 3.6 gives 28.8 km/h, so the conversion is correct.

questions.topic: Average speed from a trip log
questions.stem: A trip log shows 150 km in 3 hours including stops; what is average speed in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed uses total distance over total time, so 150 km / 3 h = 50 km/h.

questions.stem: A costing sheet proposes acceleration = distance + time; what's wrong?

options.text: Adding distance and time is dimensionally invalid.
Nothing; distance plus time is acceleration.
It should be distance minus time.
It should be distance times time.

questions.explanation: Distance has dimension L and time has T, so they cannot be added. Acceleration needs L T^-2.

questions.stem: A costing sheet uses 1/v in a formula; what are its dimensions?

options.text: T L^-1, time over length.
L T^-1, same as velocity.
L^-1 T, length inverse times time.
Dimensionless, because reciprocal cancels.

questions.explanation: The reciprocal of velocity has dimensions T L^-1. Units do not cancel in a reciprocal.
questions.hint: Invert L T^-1 to T L^-1.

questions.topic: Dimensional test of a surface formula
questions.stem: A costing sheet offers area = length * width * height; what dimension does it yield?

options.text: L^3, volume not area.
L^2, area.
L, length only.
Dimensionless.

questions.explanation: Multiplying three lengths gives L^3, volume, not area. Area needs two lengths.

questions.stem: A costing sheet lists 9.8 N/kg for an ingredient; what acceleration in m/s^2?
questions.explanation: N/kg equals m/s^2, so 9.8 N/kg = 9.8 m/s^2.

questions.stem: In the costing sheet, which time unit is derived rather than base?

options.text: Second is derived, not base.
Minute is derived; second is base.
Both second and minute are base.
Neither second nor minute is a unit.

questions.explanation: Second is the SI base unit for time; minute is derived from it. Both are units, but only second is base.

questions.stem: The costing sheet shows 500 micrograms of spice; how many grams is that?

options.text: 0.0005 grams, because micro means one millionth.
0.005 grams, treating micro as one hundred thousandth.
0.05 grams, treating micro as one ten thousandth.
0.5 grams, treating micro as one thousandth.

questions.explanation: Micro means one millionth, so 500 ug = 0.0005 g. The other options misapply the prefix.

questions.learningObjective: Convert km/h to m/s with fractions
questions.stem: A costing sheet converts 36 km/h to 10 m/s; is this correct?

options.text: Yes, 36 divided by 3.6 is 10.
No, it should be 100 m/s.
No, it should be 1 m/s.
No, it should be 0.1 m/s.

questions.explanation: Dividing 36 km/h by 3.6 gives 10 m/s, so the conversion is correct.

questions.topic: Average speed from a trip log
questions.learningObjective: Compute average speed from two legs
questions.stem: A trip log shows 60 km in 1 hour then 60 km in 2 hours; what is overall average speed in km/h?
questions.explanation: Total distance 120 km over total time 3 h gives 40 km/h.
questions.hint: Use total distance and total time.

questions.learningObjective: Check dimensional consistency of kinematic equation
questions.stem: A costing sheet states v = u + a t; is this dimensionally consistent?

options.text: Yes, all terms have dimensions L T^-1.
No, a t has dimensions L T^-2.
No, u has dimensions L T^-2.
No, v has dimensions L T^-2.

questions.explanation: Velocity u is L T^-1 and a t is (L T^-2)*T = L T^-1, so all terms match. The equation is consistent.

questions.learningObjective: Compare dimensions of speed and velocity
questions.stem: In the costing sheet, speed and velocity both have units m/s; do their dimensions differ?

options.text: Yes, velocity has an extra mass dimension.
No, both have dimensions L T^-1.
Yes, speed has L^2 T^-1.
Yes, velocity has L T^-2.

questions.explanation: Both speed and velocity are length over time, L T^-1. Dimensions are identical even though velocity is a vector.

questions.topic: Dimensional test of a surface formula
questions.stem: A costing sheet states area = length + width; what dimension does it yield?

options.text: L, not area.
L^2, area.
L^3, volume.
Dimensionless.

questions.explanation: Adding two lengths gives length L, not area L^2. Addition requires same dimensions but result keeps that dimension.

questions.learningObjective: Compute mass from force and acceleration
questions.stem: A costing sheet applies 50 N and gets 10 m/s^2; what mass in kg is involved?
questions.explanation: Mass equals force divided by acceleration, so 50 N / 10 m/s^2 = 5 kg.

questions.stem: Chef's costing sheet converts 5 minutes to 300 seconds; what validates it?

options.text: 5 times 60 seconds per minute equals 300.
5 times 100 seconds per minute equals 500.
5 times 30 seconds per minute equals 150.
5 plus 295 seconds is 300.

questions.explanation: Each minute has 60 seconds, so 5 minutes = 300 seconds. The other factors are wrong.

questions.stem: The costing sheet shows 800 nanometres of film; how many metres is that?

options.text: 0.0000008 metres, because nano means 10^-9.
0.000008 metres, treating nano as 10^-6.
0.00008 metres, treating nano as 10^-5.
0.008 metres, treating nano as 10^-3.

questions.explanation: Nano means 10^-9, so 800 nm = 0.0000008 m. The other options misapply the prefix.

questions.learningObjective: Convert m/s to km/h for a mixer
questions.stem: A costing sheet converts 12 m/s mixer speed to 43.2 km/h; correct?

options.text: Yes, 12 times 3.6 equals 43.2.
No, it should be 3.33 km/h.
No, it should be 120 km/h.
No, it should be 432 km/h.

questions.explanation: Multiplying 12 m/s by 3.6 gives 43.2 km/h, so the conversion is correct.

questions.topic: Average speed from a trip log
questions.learningObjective: Compute average speed for a round trip
questions.stem: A round trip covers 80 km out and 80 km back in 4 hours total; what is average speed in km/h?
questions.explanation: Total distance 160 km over 4 h gives 40 km/h.

questions.stem: In the costing sheet, jerk is acceleration per time; what are its dimensions?

options.text: L T^-3, length over time cubed.
L T^-2, same as acceleration.
L T^-1, same as velocity.
M L T^-3, adds mass.

questions.explanation: Jerk is acceleration divided by time, (L T^-2)/T = L T^-3. Mass is not involved.

questions.stem: A costing sheet uses momentum = mass times velocity; what are its dimensions?

options.text: M L T^-1, mass times length over time.
L T^-1, velocity only.
M L T^-2, force dimensions.
M^2 L T^-1, mass squared.

questions.explanation: Momentum is mass times velocity, M * L T^-1 = M L T^-1. Force is M L T^-2.

questions.topic: Dimensional test of a surface formula
questions.stem: A costing sheet offers volume = length * width * height; dimensions?

options.text: L^3, volume.
L^2, area.
L, length.
M L^3, adds mass.

questions.explanation: Three lengths multiply to L^3, volume. Area would be L^2.

questions.learningObjective: Compute force from mass and acceleration
questions.stem: A costing sheet has 6 kg mass with acceleration 4 m/s^2; what force in newtons?
questions.explanation: Force equals mass times acceleration, so 6 kg * 4 m/s^2 = 24 N.

questions.stem: Chef's costing sheet asks which is not a base unit for time; what is the answer?

options.text: Second is not a base unit for time.
Minute is not a base unit for time.
Hour is a base unit for time.
Day is a base unit for time.

questions.explanation: Minute, hour, and day are derived units; second is the only SI base unit for time.

questions.stem: The costing sheet lists 1 teragram of flour; how many grams is that?

options.text: 1,000,000,000,000 grams, because tera means 10^12.
1,000,000,000 grams, treating tera as giga.
1,000,000 grams, treating tera as mega.
1,000 grams, treating tera as kilo.

questions.explanation: Tera means 10^12, so 1 Tg = 1,000,000,000,000 g. The other options misapply the prefix.

questions.learningObjective: Convert km/h to m/s for a drone
questions.stem: A costing sheet converts 18 km/h drone speed to 5 m/s; correct?

options.text: Yes, 18 divided by 3.6 is 5.
No, it should be 64.8 m/s.
No, it should be 1.8 m/s.
No, it should be 0.5 m/s.

questions.explanation: Dividing 18 km/h by 3.6 gives 5 m/s, so the conversion is correct.

questions.topic: Average speed from a trip log
questions.learningObjective: Compute average speed from distance over time
questions.stem: A trip log shows 240 km in 6 hours; what is the average speed in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is 240 km / 6 h = 40 km/h.

questions.learningObjective: Check dimensions of free fall distance
questions.stem: A costing sheet uses distance = g t^2; what dimension does g t^2 have?

options.text: L, since g is L T^-2 and t^2 is T^2.
L T^-2, because t^2 is dimensionless.
T^-2, because g cancels length.
L T^2, because g is L T^-2 inverted.

questions.explanation: g has L T^-2 and t^2 has T^2, so their product is L, length. The formula is dimensionally consistent up to a factor.
questions.hint: Multiply dimensions L T^-2 by T^2.

questions.stem: A costing sheet uses kinetic energy = 0.5 m v^2; what are its dimensions?

options.text: M L^2 T^-2, mass times velocity squared.
M L T^-2, force dimensions.
M L^2 T^-1, energy rate.
L^2 T^-2, drops mass.

questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is mass times velocity squared, M * L^2 T^-2 = M L^2 T^-2. The other choices mishandle powers.
questions.hint: Square velocity and multiply by mass.

questions.topic: Dimensional test of a surface formula
questions.stem: A costing sheet proposes area = length * time; what is wrong?

options.text: Area needs length squared, not length times time.
Area needs length cubed, not length times time.
Area needs mass times length, not length times time.
Nothing; length times time is area.

questions.explanation: Area has dimensions L^2, while length times time has L T, so the formula is invalid.

questions.learningObjective: Compute acceleration from weight and mass
questions.stem: A costing sheet shows weight 39.2 N on a 4 kg mass; what acceleration in m/s^2?
questions.explanation: Acceleration equals force over mass, so 39.2 N / 4 kg = 9.8 m/s^2.

questions.stem: Chef's costing sheet converts 1 day to 86400 seconds; what validates it?

options.text: 24 hours times 60 minutes times 60 seconds.
24 hours times 100 minutes times 36 seconds.
12 hours times 60 minutes times 120 seconds.
1 day is a base unit, so no conversion.

questions.explanation: One day is 24 hours, each hour 60 minutes, each minute 60 seconds, giving 86400 seconds.

questions.stem: The costing sheet shows 4 hectograms of cheese; how many grams is that?

options.text: 40 grams, treating hecto as deca.
400 grams, because hecto means one hundred.
4000 grams, treating hecto as kilo.
4 grams, treating hecto as unit.

questions.explanation: Hecto means one hundred, so 4 hg = 400 g. The other options misapply the prefix.

questions.learningObjective: Convert m/s to km/h for a conveyor
questions.stem: A costing sheet converts 2.5 m/s conveyor speed to 9 km/h; correct?

options.text: Yes, 2.5 times 3.6 is 9.
No, it should be 0.69 km/h.
No, it should be 25 km/h.
No, it should be 90 km/h.

questions.explanation: Multiplying 2.5 m/s by 3.6 gives 9 km/h, so the conversion is correct.

questions.topic: Average speed from a trip log
questions.learningObjective: Compute average speed from total values
questions.stem: A trip log shows 300 km in 5 hours; what is the average speed in km/h?
questions.explanation: Average speed is 300 km / 5 h = 60 km/h.
